blocks.text: Cloud deployment models define how cloud services are made available and used. Each gives a different level of control, security and flexibility. The main models are public, private, hybrid and multi-cloud.

blocks.alt: Left: four columns, own PC, IaaS, PaaS and SaaS, each a stack of six layers from applications down to hardware, coloured by whether the user or the provider manages each layer. Right: one machine split into three virtual machines with notes on scalability, elasticity, on-demand access and pay as you go. Bottom: public, private, hybrid and multi-cloud boxes with examples.
blocks.caption: Cloud service models, core ideas and deployment models (original diagram after topic 6.2).
blocks.long_description: On your own computer you manage every layer. With IaaS the provider runs the hardware and virtualization while you manage the operating system, runtime, data and applications; with PaaS the provider also runs the operating system and runtime, so you manage only your data and application; with SaaS the provider runs everything and you simply use the software. Virtualization turns one physical machine into several virtual machines. Public clouds are shared and cheaper, private clouds serve one organization securely, hybrid clouds combine the two, and multi-cloud uses several providers for resilience.

blocks.prompt: Define cloud deployment models and assess the differences, with examples (long questions 2 and 8).
blocks.explanation: A deployment model says who owns the cloud and who shares it. Public: shared by many organizations and run by a provider such as AWS; cheapest and easiest to scale, but less control. Private: used by one organization, for example a bank's own data centre; most control and security, but most expensive. Hybrid: public plus private, for example everyday work in the public cloud and sensitive data in the private one, moving overflow to the public cloud at busy times; flexible. Multi-cloud: services from several providers, for example Google Cloud for analytics, Azure for business applications and AWS for backup; resilient and avoids depending on one provider.

items: Deployment: public (shared), private (one organization), hybrid (both), multi-cloud (several providers).
